output.best_reason: Version B has the most distinct and believable voice: Rosa's Emmental origin, twenty-two years in the house, her "I do not know what to do with my hands," and her wry, self-protective manner all feel lived-in. Its period detail (the sûreté inspector, the temple striking, the Morbier in the hall) reads as texture rather than pastiche. Its facts come out through her memory and emotion, so the timeline and the discovery arrive as a story she is telling, not a checklist. Version A is the closest rival and arguably the most tense, since the clock-fast gimmick turns each reading into a trap and the closing line lands hard. It loses ground because Rosa is less specific as a person, and the repeated "by my kitchen clock" phrasing starts to feel mechanical. Version C is weakest: it front-loads exposition about the master, the household and who goes up to the atelier, then delivers the forensic inventory (blood, mallet, stopped regulator, the striking watch) in one unbroken speech. It also addresses her as "Madame Häfeli" though she is a Fräulein, a continuity slip an attentive editor would flag.
